name: XRP (BPF-KV, WiredTiger patches)
baseline: read() system calls and io_uring (also SPDK)
workload: Random 512 B lookups in BPF-KV (B+-tree, 3-6 index levels on disk) and WiredTiger YCSB, O_DIRECT, Optane P5800X, resubmitting dependent I/Os from the NVMe driver with an eBPF hook
claimed_speedup: BPF-KV: 47%-94% higher throughput and 20%-34% lower p99 latency than read() (3 index levels, multi-thread); up to 1.5x over io_uring for small batches and up to 2.5x as batch size grows (single-thread); WiredTiger up to 24% under YCSB
hardware: 6-core Intel i5-8500 3 GHz, 16 GB RAM, Intel Optane SSD P5800X, Ubuntu 20.04, Linux 5.12 (hyperthreading off, turbo off, KPTI on)
tradeoffs: Needs a patched Linux 5.12 kernel; I/O request limited to 512 B, no fanout; only helps dependent-read chains (B-tree, LSM lookups) on ext4 with extent metadata cached in the NVMe driver; BPF verifier limits.
caveats: Compiler flags not stated in the paper draft (build scripts not inspected); numbers are from the OSDI'22 paper draft checked into the repo, which I opened and parsed with pdftotext. Closed-loop experiment, so XRP runs at higher throughput than the baselines in latency plots.
found_via: WebSearch: eBPF storage function NVMe driver io_uring baseline paper github artifact; opened repo README and XRP Draft.pdf via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: SplitFS
baseline: ext4 DAX (POSIX file I/O on persistent memory; NOVA also compared in paper)
workload: Appends of 4 KB chunks to a file then fsync on persistent memory (README microbenchmark), plus LevelDB, SQLite, Redis, YCSB, tar, git in the SOSP'19 paper
claimed_speedup: README: appends 5.8x faster than ext4 DAX (1.92M vs 0.33M appends/sec); up to 2x on data-intensive workloads; software overhead 4-12x lower than NOVA or ext4 DAX
hardware: Intel processor with clflush, 32 GB+ DRAM, emulated or real PM (README requirements); microbenchmark compiled gcc -O3
tradeoffs: User-space LD_PRELOAD library on top of ext4 DAX plus a patched kernel; Ubuntu 16.04/18.04; only POSIX calls intercepted via glibc; persistent memory hardware needed.
caveats: README says copyright is held by the University of Texas at Austin, contact for commercial license; no OSI license, so reference only. SOSP'19 paper PDF not opened (host blocked); the 5.8x and 4-12x figures are on the README page. README microbenchmark hardware not stated precisely.
found_via: WebSearch: persistent memory file system outperforms ext4-DAX NOVA paper github; opened repo README

name: WineFS
baseline: ext4-DAX, xfs-DAX and NOVA (kernel PM file systems); mmap workloads
workload: Memory-mapped RocksDB and LMDB workloads on a hugepage-aware persistent-memory file system, aged file system state
claimed_speedup: README: outperforms ext4-DAX, NOVA and xfs-DAX by up to 2x on RocksDB and LMDB; matches or exceeds on Filebench and WiredTiger (paper snippet: 54% over ext4-DAX, 2x over NOVA)
tradeoffs: Kernel file system for Intel Optane PM; non-commercial license; research code on old kernels.
caveats: Licence is Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial, which is not OSI-approved; reference only. SOSP'21 paper not opened (blocked); README gives only qualitative bounds. Last commit date not retrieved. Baseline is a kernel file system through POSIX or mmap, not literally the three listed baselines.
found_via: WebSearch: persistent memory file system outperforms ext4-DAX NOVA paper; opened repo page

name: NOVA (linux-nova)
baseline: ext4-DAX, xfs-DAX, PMFS, Ext4-data, Btrfs (kernel file systems on NVM)
workload: Log-structured file system for byte-addressable NVMM, Filebench and macro workloads
claimed_speedup: Paper snippet: 22% to 216x throughput improvement over state-of-the-art file systems; 3.1x-13.5x over file systems with equally strong consistency; README: in almost all cases outperforms other DAX-enabled file systems (sub-page updates are a noted exception)
tradeoffs: Kernel tree fork (Linux with NOVA in fs/nova); ties you to an old kernel; copy-on-write cost for sub-page updates.
caveats: Paper PDF host is egress-blocked in this environment; numbers quoted from search-result snippets of the paper, not from an opened page. README opened and confirms the qualitative claim; numerical figures only from the FAST'16 paper snippet. It is a Linux kernel tree, but the NOVA code itself is a distinct file system, so is_fork_of left null. Last commit date not retrieved.

name: TriCache
baseline: mmap and Linux swap (OS page cache)
workload: Out-of-core graph processing (Ligra PR, WCC, BFS), RocksDB, Terasort and LiveGraph run unmodified on a user-transparent multi-level block cache over SSDs
claimed_speedup: Paper snippet: speedups over OS swapping 6.30x on PR, 26.1x on WCC (0.85x on BFS); more than an order of magnitude over the Linux page cache in places; artifact compares against swap and mmap
hardware: 2x AMD EPYC 7742, >=512 GB RAM, 8x Intel P4618 SSDs, Debian 11.1, Linux 5.10 (artifact recommendations)
tradeoffs: Needs SPDK-style SSD access (devices get formatted), huge memory and many SSDs; BFS is slower than swap (0.85x); intrusive setup.
caveats: Paper PDF host is egress-blocked in this environment; numbers quoted from search-result snippets of the paper, not from an opened page. Repo README (osdi-ae branch) opened: it lists the compared systems and hardware but has no numbers. Compiler flags not stated. OSDI'22 paper, so tier would be B if the paper were opened.
